metrics.name: Hearing close-out rate
metrics.question: When a hearing happens, does someone record the outcome and next step on Legistify within 2 days?
metrics.why: The hearing is the heartbeat of a litigation case. If outcomes are recorded on time, Legistify is the system of record; if not, it is only a tracker and the team works from email and Excel.
metrics.decision: A drop points to who is not closing the loop (a counsel firm, a case manager), and leads to reminders, counsel self-update or AI drafting of outcomes from synced orders.
metrics.chart: Weekly line against an 80% target band, split into in-house and counsel-owned hearings
metrics.chart_why: A trend against a target shows direction and gap at once; the split shows where the gap comes from without a second chart.
metrics.definition: Share of hearings whose date has passed in the period that have an outcome or next step recorded within 2 calendar days.
metrics.formula: count(hearings with date(hearing_outcome_recorded) - hearing_date <= 2 days) / count(hearings with hearing_date in period and hearing_date <= today - 2)

metrics.name: Weekly active seats by role
metrics.question: Of the seats the customer pays for, how many people actually work on the module each week, by role?
metrics.why: Renewal depends on usage across roles. A tool used only by the legal team is easy to cut; one used by counsel and business users is hard to replace.
metrics.decision: A weak role gets targeted onboarding (counsel, business users) or a lighter surface built for it, such as email or WhatsApp actions.
metrics.chart: Horizontal bullet bars: active users against seats, one bar per role
metrics.chart_why: Bullet bars show actual against capacity per role in one glance; a pie would hide the seat count.
metrics.definition: Users with at least one meaningful action (not just a login) in a rolling 7 days, divided by provisioned seats, per role.
metrics.formula: count(distinct user_id with meaningful_action in last 7 days) / seats, grouped by role

metrics.name: AI credit runway
metrics.question: On which day of the month does this account run out of AI credits?
metrics.why: When credits run out, every AI feature stops for the whole account. The value the customer sees from AI is capped by the calendar, not by need.
metrics.decision: An early limit day leads to a cheaper model or separate pool for bulk features, usage caps per feature, or an upgrade conversation with the account manager.
metrics.chart: Cumulative credits by day of month, one line per month, with the limit as a horizontal rule
metrics.chart_why: Cumulative lines make the crossing day visible and show whether it is moving earlier month after month.
metrics.definition: Credits consumed per calendar day, accumulated within the month, against the account's monthly limit.
metrics.formula: sum(ai_request.credits) cumulative by day; limit_day = first day cumulative >= monthly_limit
metrics.alert: Projected limit day earlier than day 25
metrics.sample: Limit of 6,000 hit on day 19 in October (day 22 in September)

metrics.name: Court sync freshness
metrics.question: Is the hearing and order data the user sees today actually up to date?
metrics.why: Every downstream number, from hearing status to close-out rate, assumes the court data is fresh. Stale sync silently breaks trust.
metrics.decision: Low freshness for a court type sends engineering to fix that scraper first, ranked by how many active cases depend on it.
metrics.chart: Horizontal bars by court type with a 95% target line
metrics.chart_why: Court types are categories with very different reliability; sorted bars rank where to fix first.
metrics.definition: Share of active cases whose court data synced successfully in the last 24 hours, by court type, averaged over the last 7 daily checks.
metrics.formula: count(active cases with court_sync_run.status = success in last 24h) / count(active cases), by court_type
metrics.sample: District courts 71%, consumer forums 64% vs high courts 96%

metrics.name: Active matters
metrics.question: How many live cases is the account running, and is the book growing?
metrics.why: Context for every other number: rates mean little without the size of the book behind them. Shown as context, not as a success metric.
metrics.decision: None on its own. A sharp change prompts a check of intake and disposal before reading other metrics.
metrics.chart: Number tile with a 26-week sparkline
metrics.chart_why: One number with its trend is all that context needs; a full chart would give a size metric too much weight.
metrics.definition: Cases not disposed or archived at the end of the period.
metrics.formula: count(cases where status in (ongoing) at period end)

metrics.name: Feature stickiness
metrics.question: Which features have become a daily habit, and which are dead weight?
metrics.why: Daily features are the product's core; features nobody returns to are either broken, misplaced or not needed.
metrics.decision: High-traffic, low-stickiness features get UX work; features under 5% become candidates to merge, move or retire.
metrics.chart: Sorted horizontal bars of DAU/MAU per feature, with features under 5% marked
metrics.chart_why: One measure across many features is a ranking, so sorted bars read fastest; the 5% marker shows the cut.
metrics.definition: Daily users of a feature divided by its users in the trailing 30 days, averaged over the period (rolling DAU ÷ MAU).
metrics.formula: avg over days(distinct users of feature that day / distinct users of feature in the 30 days ending that day)
metrics.sample: My Cases 52%, hearing updates 38%; Codex 4% and Spend 2% are near dead

metrics.name: Time to first value
metrics.question: After a new user is invited, how long until they do the thing their role needs?
metrics.why: Users who do not reach their first meaningful action in the first weeks rarely come back. Counsel and business users are the at-risk roles.
metrics.decision: A long time for a role leads to a role-specific first-run flow or an invite email that lands them on their first task.
metrics.chart: Dot plot of median days per role, with the interquartile range as a line
metrics.chart_why: A few roles with a median and spread each; dots with whiskers show both without the clutter of box plots.
metrics.definition: Median days from invite to first role-specific action: Legal = first hearing outcome; Business = first followed-case view; Lawyer = first case update; Admin = first keyword group or user change.
metrics.formula: median(first_value_action.ts - user_invited.ts) by role

metrics.name: Intake suggestion funnel
metrics.question: Of the cases the system suggests from new court filings, how many get reviewed, accepted, rejected or ignored until they expire?
metrics.why: Intake is the module's front door. Ignored suggestions mean real cases can slip past; rejected ones are wasted review time.
metrics.decision: High expiry leads to better alerts or a review queue; high rejection leads to better matching (see M09).
metrics.chart: Funnel bars: suggested, reviewed, accepted (added or mapped), with deleted and expired shown as the drop-offs
metrics.chart_why: Stage counts with the drop between them are what a funnel is for.
metrics.definition: Counts of suggestions in the last 90 days by final state: added, mapped to an existing case, deleted, or expired after 90 days untouched.
metrics.formula: count(suggestion_shown); count(suggestion_triaged by action); count(suggestion_expired)

metrics.name: Intake precision by keyword group
metrics.question: Of the suggestions people review, how many are really about the company? Which keyword groups create the noise?
metrics.why: A keyword like a company or brand name also matches unrelated parties. Every false match is a case someone must open and reject.
metrics.decision: Low precision justifies entity matching (party name, CIN, address) instead of plain keywords, and helps admins prune noisy groups.
metrics.chart: Horizontal bars of precision by keyword group, labelled with suggestion volume
metrics.chart_why: Precision per category is a ranking; the volume label shows which noisy group costs the most time.
metrics.definition: Accepted suggestions (added or mapped) divided by reviewed suggestions, per keyword group, last 90 days.
metrics.formula: count(suggestion_triaged.action in (added, mapped)) / count(suggestion_triaged), by keyword_group
metrics.alert: Any group below 25% with more than 50 suggestions
metrics.sample: 31% overall; brand names 18%, company name 22%, directors' names 69%

metrics.name: Early-capture rate
metrics.question: Are new cases tracked before their first hearing, so the team is not caught off guard?
metrics.why: Catching a case before the first hearing, often before the summons, is the core promise of automated intake.
metrics.decision: A low rate for a business unit points to missing keywords for its entities or slow review, and to faster alert channels.
metrics.chart: Bars by business unit against a 75% target line
metrics.chart_why: Four units compared on one rate with a target: bars with a reference line.
metrics.definition: Share of new cases tracked (added) before their first listed hearing date, last 90 days.
metrics.formula: count(case_created.ts < first hearing_date) / count(case_created), by business_unit

metrics.name: Field completeness at day 14
metrics.question: Two weeks after a case is added, does it have the fields the GC's Insights tabs need?
metrics.why: Financials and Team & Counsel tabs are only as good as these fields. In the demo, about 1 case in 20 had exposure filled in.
metrics.decision: Low completeness leads to prompts at the moment of adding a case, required fields per role, or AI extraction of amounts from the plaint.
metrics.chart: Dumbbell per field: completeness when added and at day 14
metrics.chart_why: Two points per field show both the starting gap and how little it closes later; that change is the story.
metrics.definition: Share of cases added in the last 90 days with the field set when added, and by day 14.
metrics.formula: count(cases with field set within N days of case_created) / count(cases), for N = 0 and 14, per field
metrics.sample: Exposure 3% to 11%, risk rating 2% to 9%, counsel 41% to 63%

metrics.name: Default-priority share
metrics.question: Is priority a real judgment or a value nobody changes?
metrics.why: If nearly every case is high priority, priority cannot help anyone choose what to work on, and priority-based views are meaningless.
metrics.decision: A share above 90% supports deriving priority from exposure and hearing proximity instead of asking users.
metrics.chart: Number tile with a sparkline
metrics.chart_why: One share and its trend; nothing to compare it against.
metrics.definition: Share of active cases whose priority still equals the default set at creation.
metrics.formula: count(active cases where priority = default and never updated) / count(active cases)

metrics.name: Outcome update lag by counsel firm
metrics.question: Which counsel firms take longest to report what happened at a hearing, and how much of the docket do they carry?
metrics.why: Counsel own most hearings. One slow firm with a large share can pull the whole account's close-out rate down.
metrics.decision: A slow, high-volume firm gets an escalation through the GC, an email-reply update option, or reallocation of new matters.
metrics.chart: Scatter: median update lag (x) against on-platform activity (y), bubble size = hearings in period
metrics.chart_why: Three attributes per firm at once; the scatter puts the problem firm alone in one corner.
metrics.definition: Per firm, the median days between a hearing and its recorded outcome, counted from the start of the hearing day; on-platform activity = share of the firm's assigned cases with any action by its lawyers in 30 days.
metrics.formula: median(hearing_outcome_recorded.lag_days) by firm; count(cases with firm action in 30d) / count(firm cases)
metrics.events: hearing_outcome_recorded {firm_id, lag_days}, any action by role = Lawyer
metrics.alert: Firm median lag above 5 days with more than 20 hearings
metrics.sample: Mehra & Associates: 38% of hearings, 9.4-day lag, 22% active; others 1.8 to 2.6 days

metrics.name: Hearings awaiting update
metrics.question: Right now, which past hearings still have no outcome, and on whose desk are they?
metrics.why: This is the PM's view of the bottleneck: it turns the close-out rate into named people.
metrics.decision: A concentration on one person leads to workload rebalancing, nudges, or delegation to counsel.
metrics.chart: Ranked horizontal bars, top 10 case managers, each bar split by who owns the hearing (in-house or counsel)
metrics.chart_why: A ranked list of people is the natural drill path to the user view; the split shows if the delay is theirs or their counsel's.
metrics.definition: Hearings more than 2 days past with no outcome recorded, grouped by case manager.
metrics.formula: count(hearings where hearing_date < today - 2 and no hearing_outcome_recorded), by case_manager

metrics.name: Dormant matters
metrics.question: How many live cases have had no activity at all for 90 days?
metrics.why: Dormant cases are where hearings get missed and exposure goes unmanaged. The product promises nothing slips.
metrics.decision: A rising count makes dormancy an assigned follow-up, not a passive chart.
metrics.chart: Area chart over 26 weeks, with the share of active matters as a label
metrics.chart_why: A single quantity over time; the area emphasises the growing backlog.
metrics.definition: Active cases with no user action, task or document event for 90 or more days.
metrics.formula: count(active cases where max(activity.ts) < today - 90)

metrics.name: AI adoption vs trust by feature
metrics.question: Which AI features are used, and which are used but not trusted?
metrics.why: High use with low follow-through means people try AI but do not rely on it. That is the difference between an AI feature and an AI demo.
metrics.decision: Low trust with high use calls for output-quality work; high trust with low use calls for better placement or discovery.
metrics.chart: Quadrant scatter: adoption (x) against action rate (y), one point per AI feature, bubble size = credits used
metrics.chart_why: Two measures per feature define four clear actions; quadrants make the action readable without a legend.
metrics.definition: Adoption = share of active Legal and Lawyer users who used the feature in 30 days. Action rate = share of AI outputs followed within 10 minutes by copy, export, task, document or field edit.
metrics.formula: distinct users(ai_request.feature) / active legal+lawyer users; count(ai_output_actioned) / count(ai_response)
metrics.alert: Action rate below 25% for a feature using more than 20% of credits
metrics.sample: Ask AI 67% / 61%; AI Diligence 9% / 17% but 46% of credits

metrics.name: AI usage after the credit limit
metrics.question: What happens to AI use once the account runs out of credits?
metrics.why: Shows the cost of the limit in lost usage, which is what the account manager and pricing team need to see.
metrics.decision: A steep drop supports moving bulk features to a separate pool or cheaper model, so everyday Ask AI keeps working.
metrics.chart: Daily Ask AI queries for the current month, with the limit day marked
metrics.chart_why: A daily line with one annotated event shows the cliff better than any summary number.
metrics.definition: Ask AI requests per day, before and after the day the monthly limit is reached.
metrics.formula: count(ai_request where feature = ask_ai) by day; compare mean before and after limit_day
metrics.sample: 40 queries a day before the limit, 3 attempts a day after (down 93%)

metrics.name: Answer rejection signals
metrics.question: How often do users reject AI answers outright?
metrics.why: Regenerations and thumbs-down are the cheapest live signals of AI quality, available every day.
metrics.decision: A rise after a model or prompt change triggers rollback or a deeper evaluation of that change.
metrics.chart: Two weekly lines: regenerate rate and thumbs-down rate, with model changes marked
metrics.chart_why: Two rates over time with release markers show cause and effect.
metrics.definition: Share of AI responses regenerated, and share given a thumbs-down, per week.
metrics.formula: count(ai_feedback.type = regenerate) / count(ai_response); same for thumbs_down

metrics.name: Summary accuracy (evaluation)
metrics.question: Are AI case summaries factually right?
metrics.why: A wrong date or party in a summary can mislead a legal decision. Usage signals cannot catch this; only evaluation can.
metrics.decision: Accuracy below target blocks new AI features from release and triggers prompt or model changes.
metrics.chart: Weekly line of sampled accuracy with a 90% target line
metrics.chart_why: A quality score over time against a bar to clear.
metrics.definition: Phase 1: a reviewer grades 50 random summaries a week against the source documents (parties, dates, stage, relief, next hearing). Phase 2: an AI grader, checked against the human grades, scores every summary.
metrics.formula: correct facts / facts checked across the weekly sample

metrics.name: Insight follow-through (proxy)
metrics.question: Do the AI-written insights under Insights charts lead anyone to look closer?
metrics.why: Insights are plain text today. If nobody follows them up, they are decoration; if people do, making them clickable is worth building.
metrics.decision: A meaningful rate supports turning insights into links to the filtered case list.
metrics.chart: Number tile with a 12-week sparkline
metrics.chart_why: A single proxy rate; showing more would claim more precision than it has.
metrics.definition: Share of Insights sessions in which the user opens a case list filtered on the dimension an insight names, within 10 minutes.
metrics.formula: count(insights sessions with case_list_opened matching viewed insight) / count(insights sessions)

metrics.name: Insights and MIS reach
metrics.question: Do the GC and finance actually use the reporting built for them?
metrics.why: Reporting is what the buyer (the GC) sees. If they do not open it, the renewal case rests on the legal team alone.
metrics.decision: Low reach from the GC leads to a scheduled email digest, or reporting placed where they already are.
metrics.chart: Weekly stacked bars of Insights viewers by role, with MIS downloads as a line
metrics.chart_why: Viewers by role are parts of a whole each week; the line adds the export habit without a second chart.
metrics.definition: Distinct weekly viewers of any Insights tab by role, plus MIS downloads per week (including AI analysis reports).
metrics.formula: distinct users(insight_viewed) by week and role; count(mis_downloaded) by week
metrics.sample: 9 viewers a week; 64 MIS downloads in October, 48 with an AI report

metrics.name: Business-user alert follow-through
metrics.question: When a business user gets an alert about a case in their unit, do they open the case?
metrics.why: Business users are the long tail of seats and mostly interact through alerts. An ignored alert is a seat with no value.
metrics.decision: Low follow-through leads to fewer, sharper alerts and a summary inside the alert itself.
metrics.chart: Bars by business unit
metrics.chart_why: Four units compared on one rate.
metrics.definition: Share of alerts opened by Business-role users that lead to a case view within 24 hours.
metrics.formula: count(alert_opened followed by case_viewed within 24h) / count(alert_sent), Business role, by business_unit

metrics.name: Spend capture
metrics.question: Is legal spend recorded against cases on the platform?
metrics.why: Spend is half of the Financials story. In the demo, the invoice count read 0 while amounts showed, so this data is fragile.
metrics.decision: Low capture supports counsel invoice upload or a link to the company's finance system.
metrics.chart: Number tile plus bars by business unit
metrics.chart_why: The headline share and where it is weakest.
metrics.definition: Share of active cases with at least one spend or invoice entry in the last 90 days.
metrics.formula: count(active cases with spend_logged in 90d) / count(active cases)

metrics.name: Contract-dispute share
metrics.question: How many litigation cases arise from a contract, and so could be linked to the contract in CLM?
metrics.why: Sizes the opportunity behind Legistify's unified CLM and litigation thesis. After a 'link to contract' feature ships, this becomes 'share of cases linked to a contract'.
metrics.decision: A large share justifies building the contract link and the cross-module views it enables.
metrics.chart: Bars by business unit, with the account average marked
metrics.chart_why: One share across four units with a reference.
metrics.definition: Share of active cases whose case type is contract-based (dealer, vendor, commercial, employment contract).
metrics.formula: count(active cases where case_type in contract_types) / count(active cases), by business_unit

metrics.name: Page load time (p95)
metrics.question: Are the pages people use daily fast enough?
metrics.why: A slow Insights tab is a quiet reason the GC stops opening it. In the demo, several screens sat on loading skeletons.
metrics.decision: Pages over budget get performance work ahead of new features.
metrics.chart: Horizontal bars per page against a 3-second budget line
metrics.chart_why: A few pages compared to one budget.
metrics.definition: 95th percentile time to interactive per page, last 7 days.
metrics.formula: p95(page_loaded.load_ms) by page
metrics.sample: Insights 6.8 s, Codex 4.1 s, My Cases 2.4 s, case page 1.9 s

metrics.name: Rate-limit errors
metrics.question: How often do users hit 'Rate limit exceeded' while working?
metrics.why: Seen repeatedly in the demo. Every error interrupts a task and makes the product feel broken.
metrics.decision: Peaks at busy times justify raising limits or caching on the heaviest calls.
metrics.chart: Daily line of errors per 100 sessions, Mondays marked
metrics.chart_why: A daily rate over time; the Monday markers show the pattern.
metrics.definition: HTTP 429 responses seen by users per 100 sessions.
metrics.formula: count(api_error.code = 429) / count(session_started) * 100

metrics.name: Zero-result searches
metrics.question: What are people searching for and not finding?
metrics.why: A search with no results is a user telling us what is missing, from a court not covered to a query Codex cannot answer.
metrics.decision: Frequent misses feed court coverage priorities and Codex prompt and data improvements.
metrics.chart: Two bars (court search, Codex) with the top missed queries listed beside them
metrics.chart_why: Two surfaces compared; the query list is what someone can act on.
metrics.definition: Share of searches returning no results, by surface.
metrics.formula: count(search_performed.results_count = 0) / count(search_performed), by surface

user_only.name: Activity heatmap
user_only.question: When does this person work on the module?
user_only.chart: Day-of-week by hour grid, last 8 weeks
user_only.chart_why: Shows habit at a glance and whether work bunches before hearing days.

user_only.name: Recent activity timeline
user_only.question: What did they do recently?
user_only.chart: Vertical timeline of the last 20 actions
user_only.chart_why: The quickest way for support or a PM to see a person's real workflow.

user_only.name: Compared with team median
user_only.question: Is this person above or below their team on the key rates?
user_only.chart: Small bars with a team-median tick for M01, M11, M14, M16
user_only.chart_why: A tick on each bar compares without a second chart.

breakdowns.question: What is in the expired pile, and how soon do reviews happen?
breakdowns.why: Shows whether expired suggestions were noise or missed cases, which decides between reviewing more and ranking better.

breakdowns.question: Whose hearings are they, and how long have they waited?
breakdowns.why: Separates one firm's backlog from a general habit, and shows how stale the oldest items are.

breakdowns.question: Which units hold them, and how long have they been quiet?
breakdowns.why: Shows whether dormancy comes from missing counsel or from neglect, which need different fixes.

breakdowns.question: How many credits does each used output cost, and who runs AI Diligence?
breakdowns.why: Turns trust into cost, so pricing and model choices can be made per feature.

breakdowns.question: Where do alerts drop: sent, opened, or case viewed?
breakdowns.why: Shows whether to fix the alert itself or the case page it leads to.
